title: To the Ends of the Earth
subtitle: Acts in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Acts begins with a cloud and ends with an open door. In between: wind and fire in an upper room, a beggar leaping through a temple gate, a desert road, a blinding light, a basket over a wall, midnight singing in a prison, a shipwreck, and a small rented house in Rome.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts, following the good news from Jerusalem outward to the ends of the earth. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the story left behind—a mat on a step, a pile of cloaks, a belt, four anchors—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the book of Acts alongside this one, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: taken up
paintings.epigraph: “a cloud received him out of their sight.”
paintings.poem:
he didn't vanish.
he didn't fade.

he rose,
slow enough to watch,
until a cloud
folded him in.

the last thing they saw
was not a goodbye.

it was a promise
going up
ahead of them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “taken up” (Acts 1:9)—where the poem notes, “going up ahead of them”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: why stand looking
paintings.epigraph: “why do you stand looking into the sky?”
paintings.poem:
it's a fair question,
and a kind one.

he's coming back.
the same way
you saw him go.

so you can stop
staring at the clouds.

there's a city
down the hill,
and a promise
to wait for.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 1:11 (“and a promise to wait for”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: one accord
paintings.epigraph: “All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication”
paintings.poem:
they didn't
have a plan.

they had a room,
and each other,
and the last thing
he told them.

so they prayed.
the fishermen,
the women,
his mother,
his brothers who
hadn't believed him before.

ten days
of waiting together.

sometimes that's
the whole assignment.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 1:14 (“sometimes that's the whole assignment”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: wind
paintings.epigraph: “Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.”
paintings.poem:
first, a sound.

not a whisper.
not a breeze.

a rushing
that filled the house
from the floor
to the rafters.

the same breath
that moved over the waters
in the beginning

came back
to fill a room
full of ordinary people.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 2:2 (“to fill a room full of ordinary people”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: tongues like fire
paintings.epigraph: “T ongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them.”
paintings.poem:
not one great fire
over the crowd.

a flame for each.

the one who denied him.
the one who doubted.
the quiet ones
whose names
we barely know.

no one was left out.
no one got
a bigger portion.

one sat on each of them.

one is sitting
on you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “tongues like fire” (Acts 2:3)—where the poem notes, “one is sitting on you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: his own language
paintings.epigraph: “everyone heard them speaking in his own language.”
paintings.poem:
at Babel
the languages
scattered us.

at Pentecost
God used them
to gather us back.

no one had to
learn the right words first.

he came
in the words
they already had.

he still speaks
your language.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “his own language” (Acts 2:6)—where the poem notes, “he still speaks your language”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: cut to the heart
paintings.epigraph: “they were cut to the heart”
paintings.poem:
it wasn't a trick.
no one was argued
into the kingdom.

they heard the truth
about the one they'd crucified,

and it went in
like a blade
and opened them.

brothers, what shall we do?

that question
is where
every new life starts.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37)—where the poem notes, “is where every new life starts”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: breaking bread at home
paintings.epigraph: “breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart”
paintings.poem:
three thousand people
in one day,

and the church
started at the table.

not a building.
not a stage.
a loaf,
torn and passed,
house to house.

glad hearts.
simple food.

every kitchen
became a sanctuary.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (Acts 2:46)?

paintings.title: the gate called Beautiful
paintings.epigraph: “whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful”
paintings.poem:
every day
they carried him
to the gate called Beautiful

and left him there,
outside,
with a bowl.

more than forty years old,
still at the doorway
of the house of God,

close enough
to hear the singing,
never once
walking in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “the gate called Beautiful” (Acts 3:2), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: silver and gold
paintings.epigraph: “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you.”
paintings.poem:
he held out his bowl
for a coin.

Peter didn't
have one.

he had something else.

and it's still true:
you may not have
what they're asking for.

but if you've been
with Jesus,

you have
what they need.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “silver and gold” (Acts 3:6)—where the poem notes, “you have what they need”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: walking, leaping
paintings.epigraph: “Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.”
paintings.poem:
he left his mat
on the step.

he wouldn't
need it anymore.

and for the first time
in his life
he went through the gate,

not quietly,
not politely,

leaping.

some praise
can't stay
in its seat.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “walking, leaping” (Acts 3:8)—where the poem notes, “can't stay in its seat”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: they had been with Jesus
paintings.epigraph: “They recognized that they had been with Jesus.”
paintings.poem:
no schooling.
no titles.
fishermen's hands
in a room full of scholars.

and still,
the council noticed
something.

it wasn't
their education.
it was their company.

you become
like the one
you spend your time with.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13)—where the poem notes, “like the one you spend your time with”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: shaken
paintings.epigraph: “When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together.”
paintings.poem:
they'd just been threatened.
told to stop.

so they prayed—
not for safety.
for boldness.

and the room
answered.

the walls shook.
the lamps swung.

their fear
did not.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Acts 4:31?

paintings.title: son of encouragement
paintings.epigraph: “having a field, sold it and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.”
paintings.poem:
his name was Joses.

they called him Barnabas,
son of encouragement,

which tells you
what it was like
to be around him.

he sold a field
and laid the money down
and walked away
lighter.

later he'd vouch
for a man no one trusted.

encouragers
give their land
and their reputation.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Acts 4:36–37?

paintings.title: his shadow
paintings.epigraph: “so that as Peter came by, at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them.”
paintings.poem:
they lined the street
with cots and mattresses
and waited
for him to pass.

just his shadow.
that was enough for them.

not because Peter
was anything special.

he'd walked beside
the one
who is.

and it had rubbed off
on his shadow.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 5:15 (“and it had rubbed off on his shadow”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: fell asleep
paintings.epigraph: “The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.”
paintings.poem:
he saw heaven open
and Jesus standing,
standing,
as if to welcome him.

and with the stones
coming down
he knelt and prayed
for the ones throwing them.

then he fell asleep.

and a young man named Saul
watched their cloaks
and heard every word.

no prayer like that
is ever wasted.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “fell asleep” (Acts 7:58–60) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: scattered
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.”
paintings.poem:
the persecution meant
to stamp them out.

it only
spread them out.

like a hand
opening over a field,

every family
that ran from Jerusalem
carried the story
in their mouths.

you can't
kill a seed
by scattering it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “scattered” (Acts 8:1–4)—where the poem notes, “kill a seed by scattering it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: do you understand
paintings.epigraph: “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?”
paintings.poem:
a desert road.
a court official
reading Isaiah out loud
and not getting it.

and a man who'd been
in the middle of a revival
sent all the way out here
for one person.

God will
cross a desert
for one honest question.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “do you understand” (Acts 8:26–31)—where the poem notes, “cross a desert for one honest question”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: here is water
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
paintings.poem:
a eunuch.
a foreigner.
a man who'd been told
all his life
what kept him out.

and now he asks it:
what's keeping me?

and the answer
is nothing.

he went on his way
rejoicing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of Acts 8:36–39?

paintings.title: light from the sky
paintings.epigraph: “suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.”
paintings.poem:
he was on the road
with letters
to arrest them
in his bag.

he knew exactly
who he was
and what he was doing.

then the light.

and a voice
that didn't say
who are you persecuting?

it said:
why do you persecute me?

every wound
he gave the church

landed on Jesus.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Acts 9:3–5)?

paintings.title: Brother Saul
paintings.epigraph: “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me”
paintings.poem:
Ananias knew
exactly who he was.

he'd heard
what this man had done.

and still
he walked in,
laid his hands on him,

and the first word
out of his mouth
was brother.

sometimes obedience
looks like
opening the door
to the one you feared.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Acts 9:17?

paintings.title: the basket
paintings.epigraph: “lowering him in a basket.”
paintings.poem:
the great apostle's
first escape

was not a miracle.

it was a rope,
a basket,
and friends
holding on in the dark.

before he carried
the gospel to the nations

he had to be
carried himself.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the basket” (Acts 9:25)—where the poem notes, “he had to be carried himself”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the coats she made
paintings.epigraph: “showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.”
paintings.poem:
when she died
the widows didn't
give speeches.

they held up
the coats.

every seam
a kindness.
every garment
someone was wearing
because of her.

and then Peter knelt
and said
Tabitha, get up.

and she did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the coats she made” (Acts 9:39–40)—where the poem notes, “and she did”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the great sheet
paintings.epigraph: “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”
paintings.poem:
three times the sheet
came down.

three times Peter
said never.

he'd kept the rules
his whole life.
he wasn't about to
change now.

then the knock at the door.
a Roman's servants,
asking for him.

the vision wasn't
about food.

it was about
who's welcome
at the table.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “the great sheet” (Acts 10:11–15), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: Rhoda at the gate
paintings.epigraph: “But Peter continued knocking.”
paintings.poem:
they were praying
for Peter's release,

and when he knocked,
nobody believed it.

Rhoda was so happy
she forgot to open the gate.

and Peter just
stood there,
knocking.

sometimes the answer
comes while we're still asking,

and we
leave it waiting outside.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “Rhoda at the gate” (Acts 12:14–16), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: set apart
paintings.epigraph: “they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.”
paintings.poem:
it didn't start
with a strategy.

it started with
people praying,
and a whisper:
set them apart.

so they laid their hands
on their best two
and gave them away.

a church grows
by what it sends.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 13:2–3 (“a church grows by what it sends”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: come over and help us
paintings.epigraph: “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”
paintings.poem:
every door
had closed.

Asia, no.
Bithynia, no.

and then a dream:
a man standing across the sea
asking for help.

sometimes the no's
are how God
points you
to the yes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come over and help us” (Acts 16:9)—where the poem notes, “points you to the yes”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: seller of purple
paintings.epigraph: “The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.”
paintings.poem:
a riverbank.
a few women praying.
no synagogue.

Lydia was a businesswoman
who sold the color of kings.

she listened,
and the Lord
opened her heart.

that's the order.
he opens.
we hear.

and her house
became the first church
in Europe.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 16:14–15 (“became the first church in Europe”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: midnight
paintings.epigraph: “about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.”
paintings.poem:
beaten.
locked in stocks
in the inner cell.

and at midnight
they sang.

not after the rescue.
before.

the other prisoners
were listening.

someone always is.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 16:25–26 (“someone always is”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: what must I do
paintings.epigraph: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
paintings.poem:
the jailer
was ready to die.

the doors were open.
he thought
everyone was gone.

but nobody had run.

and the man
who'd locked them up
fell down and asked
the only question that matters.

that night
he washed their wounds,
and they baptized
his whole house.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “what must I do” (Acts 16:30–31)—where the poem notes, “and they baptized his whole house”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not far
paintings.epigraph: “he is not far from each one of us.”
paintings.poem:
a city full of altars,
and one of them
built just in case

to a god
they didn't know.

Paul didn't mock it.
he read it
as a longing.

you've been reaching for someone
your whole life.

he is not far.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not far” (Acts 17:27)—where the poem notes, “he is not far”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: tent makers
paintings.epigraph: “for by trade they were tent makers.”
paintings.poem:
between sermons
he sewed tents.

goat hair
and leather,
with Priscilla and Aquila
in a little shop in Corinth.

the gospel
didn't only happen
in the synagogue.

it happened
over the workbench,

in ordinary hours,
with calloused hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “tent makers” (Acts 18:3)—where the poem notes, “in ordinary hours, with calloused hands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the books burned
paintings.epigraph: “brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all.”
paintings.poem:
fifty thousand
pieces of silver,

going up in smoke
in the town square.

no one forced them.
they carried their spells out
themselves.

when something
takes hold of your life,
you don't sell it.
you don't store it.

you burn it.

and the word of the Lord
kept growing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the books burned” (Acts 19:19–20)—where the poem notes, “and the word of the Lord kept growing”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the window
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”
paintings.poem:
Paul preached
past midnight.

and a young man
in the window
fell asleep,
and fell.

let's be honest:
the sermon
was too long.

but grace
went downstairs,
held him close,

and the meeting went on
until sunrise.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the window” (Acts 20:9–10)—where the poem notes, “and the meeting went on until sunrise”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: more blessed to give
paintings.epigraph: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
paintings.poem:
he showed them his hands.

these worked
for your food.
these carried
what you needed.

then he gave them
words of Jesus
none of the gospels
wrote down.

and they wept
on the sand,

knowing they
wouldn't see him again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “more blessed to give” (Acts 20:35–37)—where the poem notes, “knowing they wouldn't see him again”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the belt
paintings.epigraph: “For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
paintings.poem:
a prophet
tied his own hands
with Paul's belt.

this is what's waiting.

and his friends begged him
not to go.

but some roads
you walk
knowing
where they lead.

he did.
so did Jesus.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 21:11–13 (“he did. so did Jesus”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: four anchors
paintings.epigraph: “they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight.”
paintings.poem:
no sun.
no stars.
fourteen days of storm.

so they did
the only thing left.

they dropped
four anchors
and wished for daylight.

some nights
that's all faith is:

holding on
and waiting
for morning.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 27:29 (“and waiting for morning”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: bread in the storm
paintings.epigraph: “he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, then he broke it and began to eat.”
paintings.poem:
two hundred and seventy-six
soaked and starving people,

and a prisoner
stands up
in the storm

and gives thanks.

not for the storm.
for the bread.
for the promise.

then he eats.

and they all
took courage.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (Acts 27:35)?

paintings.title: the viper
paintings.epigraph: “However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.”
paintings.poem:
shipwrecked.
soaked.
gathering sticks
like everybody else.

and then the bite.

they waited
for him to swell up
and die.

he just
shook it off
into the fire.

some things
that fasten on you
don't get the last word.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Acts 28:3–5 (“that fasten on you don't get the last word”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: without hindrance
paintings.epigraph: “preaching God’s Kingdom, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.”
paintings.poem:
the book doesn't end
with a trial
or a verdict.

it ends
with an open door.

a chained man
in a rented house,
welcoming
everyone who came.

without hindrance.

and the story
isn't finished.

it's still being written

by everyone
who walks through that door.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “without hindrance” (Acts 28:30–31)—where the poem notes, “by everyone who walks through that door”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?
